S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.

subtypes.Initial Insomnia: Difficulty falling asleep and taking a long time to do so.
subtypes.Middle Insomnia: Waking up frequently during sleep or having difficulty falling back asleep.
subtypes.Early Morning Awakening: Waking up too early and being unable to fall back asleep.
subtypes.Hypersomnia: Sleeping for long periods at night or excessive sleep during the day.
subtypes.Nightmare Disorder: Sleep disturbance caused by repeated and distressing dreams.
subtypes.Non-Restorative Sleep: Feeling unrefreshed despite having slept enough.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.

subtypes.Intrusive Memories: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Distressing Dreams: Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event.
subtypes.Dissociative Reactions (Flashbacks): Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event were recurring.
subtypes.Psychological Distress at Cues: Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Physiological Reactions to Cues: Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.

subtypes.Internal Avoidance: Efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event.
subtypes.External Avoidance: Efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).

subtypes.Fragmented Memory: Inability to recall only specific parts of the traumatic event while remembering others.
subtypes.Generalized Amnesia: Inability to recall the majority or the entirety of the traumatic event.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.

subtypes.Impulsive Anger: Sudden explosions of anger for trivial reasons or no clear reason.
subtypes.Verbal Aggression: Attacking others with shouting, cursing, or blame without holding back.
subtypes.Physical Aggression: Physically attacking people or throwing/breaking objects.
subtypes.Chronic Irritability: A state where nerves are always sharp and sensitive, ready to explode at the slightest touch.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.

subtypes.Auditory Startle: Startling excessively and flinching physically at sudden noises.
subtypes.Tactile Startle: Being extremely startled by unexpected physical contact.
subtypes.Visual Startle: Being greatly startled and wary of sudden appearances of people or rapid movements.
subtypes.Slow Recovery: Heart pounding and trembling for a long time after being startled, not calming down easily.

symptom.disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to an actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly, as a witness, or by learning about it occurring to a close other. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusive recollections, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal symptoms that last from 3 days to up to 1 month after the traumatic event and cause significant distress or functional impairment. Clinically, ASD often presents with marked anxiety, sleep disruption, and a sense of being "on edge" or emotionally numb in the immediate aftermath of trauma. It is distinguished from Posttraumatic Stress Disorder primarily by its shorter duration and more prominent acute dissociative features, and it may resolve spontaneously or progress to PTSD if symptoms persist beyond one month.

patient.personality: She is a highly detail-oriented, anxious young woman who relies on strict routines, careful budgeting, and quiet creative hobbies to feel in control of her life.
patient.stressor: Two weeks before presentation, Irma was riding home from a late shift at the community health clinic with her older cousin when another car ran a red light and T-boned their vehicle; Irma remained conscious, trapped in the passenger seat, while her cousin was critically injured and had to be extricated in front of her. Accustomed to planning and controlling every detail, she felt utterly helpless as paramedics worked on her cousin and she sat in the wreckage hearing sounds of metal, glass, and sirens, later being discharged from the emergency department with only minor physical injuries. Over the following week, her usual coping routines—journaling, crocheting, meal planning—began to fall apart as she found herself unable to return to her normal bus routes or even walk past busy intersections, and she stopped volunteering at the clinic because she could not tolerate being near the entrance where ambulances arrived. Her mother finally insisted she seek psychiatric care when Irma, exhausted and increasingly irritable, admitted she could not concentrate on basic tasks at home because her mind kept "going back" to the crash whenever she tried to relax or plan her day.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since the car accident, my mind keeps replaying it over and over, even when I don’t want to think about it.”

S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.
S027.manifestation: All week I’ve been lying in bed exhausted but as soon as I close my eyes I’m wide awake for hours, replaying the crash, and even when I finally do doze off I jerk awake from these awful dreams about sirens and metal smashing and feel more tired than before I went to bed.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
S069.manifestation: It’s like my brain keeps hitting a replay button I can’t shut off—I'll be just trying to write in my journal or watch a show and suddenly I’m back in the car, hearing the crunch of the impact and my cousin gasping, and my chest tightens and I can’t think about anything else.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.
S070.manifestation: I plan my whole day around not having to go near busy streets or the clinic, and if my mom even starts talking about the accident or asks how my cousin looked in the hospital, I shut her down or leave the room because I feel like I’ll fall apart if I let myself go there.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).
S071.manifestation: What really bothers me is that there’s this blank spot in my memory of the accident—I remember the other car’s headlights and then my cousin not answering me, but I can’t recall exactly how I got out or what the paramedics said, like my mind just skipped that part.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.
S077.manifestation: I’ve been snapping at everyone over the smallest things—if my little brother leaves a dish in the sink or my mom asks me again if I’m okay, I just explode and yell at them, and then I feel guilty but in the moment I’m so on edge I can’t hold it in.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.
S080.manifestation: Now even tiny things make me jump out of my skin—if a bus honks outside or someone drops a pan in the kitchen, my whole body jerks, my heart races like crazy, and it takes a long time for me to calm down again.
